episode_title: 276. How to build a morning routine that makes room for joy

real_qa.q: What is the yellow morning concept and how does it help people find joy outside of work?
real_qa.r: Yellow Mornings is about using your morning to make time for your yellows—the things that light you up and bring you joy outside of work. Claire Edwards coined the term yellows to describe these creative pursuits and hobbies that build your identity outside of work. By doing yoga, podcasting, journaling, and other fulfilling activities in the morning when you have the most energy, you can fuel yourself and show up better in all other areas of your life.
real_qa.requete: what is yellow mornings concept Claire Edwards

real_qa.q: How can busy nine-to-five workers find time for morning routines and personal fulfillment with limited energy?
real_qa.r: Instead of trying to add more to your day, identify low-value activities you can remove or swap out—such as scrolling on social media, checking work email at 6 a.m., or non-value-added tasks. You could swap 15 minutes of scrolling for 15 minutes of journaling. It's about energy management rather than time management: using your freshest energy on priorities that matter most, and placing lower-energy activities in the evening to create space in the morning for what you want to do.
real_qa.requete: how to find time morning routine busy nine to five workers

real_qa.q: What is an anchor activity and how can it help on the busiest days?
real_qa.r: An anchor activity is something you can do from 30 seconds to five minutes in the morning before work that brings you joy and fuels you. It could be taking a moment in the shower to breathe, writing down what you're thankful for, or setting your intention for the day. Even on the busiest days or hardest seasons, an anchor activity helps you ground yourself and reconnect with who you are before moving forward.
real_qa.requete: anchor activity morning routine Claire Edwards

real_qa.q: How did Claire Edwards write her book Yellow Mornings while working full-time in supply chain?
real_qa.r: Claire Edwards wrote 95 percent of Yellow Mornings between 6:30 and 8 a.m. before going to work. She completed her entire first draft in approximately four months while enrolled in Stacy Ennis's Idea to Draft program. She was able to move quickly because she had already been writing for over seven years through newsletters and other projects, giving her an established writing routine.
real_qa.requete: Claire Edwards Yellow Mornings book writing full-time job

real_qa.q: What obstacles did Claire Edwards face during the editing phase of her book?
real_qa.r: Claire Edwards fell into a perfectionist trap during editing, viewing the book as her entire identity and feeling pressure for it to be perfect. She edited the full manuscript three times before handing it to her editor, which she later recognized as one too many and an energy drain. She found herself caught between wanting the book to be good while also needing to manage her perfectionism.
real_qa.requete: Claire Edwards editing perfectionism book Yellow Mornings

guest.bio_context: Claire Edwards is an author and speaker who helps nine-to-five workers unlock work-life balance through morning routines. She has been writing for over seven years through newsletters and other projects. She delivered a TEDx talk and is the author of the forthcoming book Yellow Mornings, which guides readers through breaking the eat-sleep-work cycle and finding joy one morning at a time.
